items.title: Louie Bellson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I like them, and I want to do a lot of things for them. I don’t want to fight with them, because they’re seasoned players. How am I going to fight with somebody like Blue Mitchell or Conte Candoli or Pete Christlieb or Ernie Wilkins?

ctx.x: We were talking about your achievements in the ’60s. The James Brown recording was in November of ’69. If you could talk about some other achievements during this period of the ’60s, when you were leading your band – if you could talk about that, then I want to ask you about what it’s like to be a bandleader, what motivated you to assume that role.

I feel, myself, I was ready to be a bandleader because I had experience with other bandleaders. I watched and listened to what they did, how they conducted themselves with their men, with their players. So I was ready to take my own band out. Also, I had respect from my guys, because knowing that I could rehearse the band on one of my charts, I didn’t need somebody else to come in and clear up all the bad notes or whatever. They knew that I was a musician – not only a drummer, but a musician. That made me feel…

Being a bandleader, my door was always open for problems off the bandstand and around the bandstand too. I used to talk about this with Buddy Rich all the time. Buddy would yell and scream at his guys. I said, “You’re not going to get anywhere doing that.” He said, “Yes, but what do you do?” I said, “I don’t yell and scream at them, because they’re grown up. They’re players. They know how to do it.” “You’re different than I am.” I said, “That’s true.”

items.title: Louie Bellson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 12, 1996
items.q: Pete Christlieb, another sax player, Ricky Woodard now just joined us

ctx.x: Well you’ve been able to employ some pretty hot sidemen with your own band, in addition to your own arranging, you’ve had some great contributions from people. Don Menza you mentioned—

Don Menza, a marvelous, a great player. He’s borderline genius too, he really is. He’s something else. He’s a great player. Pete Christlieb, another sax player, Ricky Woodard now just joined us, and he’s another great saxophone player. I got Conte Condoli playing with us and his brother, and oh just Carl Fontana works with us now and then, Frank Strazzeri on piano, John Heard on bass. And now I have three bands you know. I have my New York band, a Chicago band and an L.A. band. Because if I get a gig in New York,…
Yeah, sure do. I recently heard the Slide Hampton Big Band in New York and the way they have some adventuresome writing there.
